claims.text: Kiln firing turns soft, pliable clay into a durable, permanent ceramic form by heating it to high temperatures inside a kiln.
claims.label: clay made permanent by heat

claims.text: The first stage, bisque firing, typically takes place at around 1830°F (1000°C).
claims.label: the 1830°F bisque firing

claims.text: Bisque firing dries and shrinks the clay into a hard, porous body, removing almost all the remaining water and beginning to fuse the clay particles.
claims.label: the hard, porous bisque body

claims.text: The later glaze firing is much hotter, often reaching 2000°F (1100°C) or more depending on the glaze composition.
claims.label: the hotter glaze firing

claims.text: That extreme heat melts the glaze into a glassy decorative surface that bonds strongly to the fired clay beneath.
claims.label: the glassy bonded glaze surface

claims.text: Throughout the firing the potter monitors and adjusts temperature, atmosphere (oxidation or reduction) and firing rate, which shape the colour, texture and appearance of the finished piece.
claims.label: the potter's control of atmosphere and rate

claims.text: Proper firing is essential to make the piece strong, durable and resistant to cracking or warping.
claims.label: firing for strength against cracking
